decision_changing_questions.question: How many rows are in the item table and how skewed is ownership?
Are login and recovery exposed publicly without a rate-limiting proxy?

root_causes.description: Missing index supporting owner-scoped item access paths
Pooled connection and worker thread held across slow non-DB work

findings.problem: item.owner_id has a foreign key but no index in the model or any migration, yet GET /items/ filters, counts and sorts by it for every non-superuser, and user deletion cascades through it.
findings.performance_principle: A lookup by a non-key attribute over a growing set must be served by an access path whose cost does not grow with the whole table.

evidence.statement: Item.owner_id is declared with foreign_key, nullable=False, ondelete=CASCADE and no index=True (contrast User.email, which has index=True).
read_items runs SELECT count(*) ... WHERE owner_id = :id and SELECT ... WHERE owner_id = :id ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET/LIMIT on every call for non-superusers.
The only create_index call in all migrations is ix_user_email; no index on item.owner_id or item.created_at was ever created.
delete_user issues DELETE FROM item WHERE owner_id = :id, and the FK is ON DELETE CASCADE, both needing the same lookup.
No runtime evidence (EXPLAIN, slow-query log, benchmark) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Matters once the item table is large enough that a sequential scan is noticeably slower than an index lookup (assumed: tens of thousands of rows or more across all users; the row count is unknown). Negligible for a starter-sized dataset. Amplification 2x is derived from the two statements (count + page) per request.

counter_evidence.statement: PostgreSQL does not auto-create an index on referencing FK columns; no migration or model adds one. The planner can still choose a cheap scan on tiny tables.
Searched repo for any other index definition (Index(, create_index, index=True): only User.email found.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: This is a template; most deployments have few items per user and a small table, where a sequential scan of a few pages is as fast as an index lookup.
findings.recommendation: Add a composite index on item (owner_id, created_at DESC) via an Alembic migration (index=True on the field alone covers the filter and cascade but not the sort). This removes the table-wide scan from the filter, count, ORDER BY and cascade-delete paths.

alternatives.why: Fixes filter/count/cascade but leaves a sort of each user's rows.
Serves filter, count and ordered page from one structure.
Masks the scan, adds invalidation; not justified without hit-rate data.

findings.trade_offs: Slightly slower item inserts/updates and extra storage; migration on a large existing table should use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid write locks.

validation.metric: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) plan node for the owner_id filter on GET /items/ queries (Seq Scan vs Index Scan) and p95 endpoint latency
validation.expectation: Seq Scan on item becomes Index Scan; buffers read per request drop for users owning a small share of the table.
validation.falsifier: The plan already uses an index (e.g. one added outside the repository) or the table is small enough that execution time is unchanged.
validation.guard: Migration test or CI check asserting the index exists; slow-query alert on item queries.

findings.problem: Unauthenticated and authenticated endpoints run memory-hard Argon2 hashing and blocking SMTP sends inside sync handlers while a request-scoped DB session (with its checked-out connection and open transaction) is held, tying up a worker thread and a pooled connection for the duration.
findings.performance_principle: Shared, scarce resources (pooled connections, worker threads) should not be held across slow work that does not need them; CPU-heavy or remote-latency work should be bounded and isolated.

evidence.statement: authenticate queries the user (opening a transaction on the session-held connection) then calls verify_password (Argon2) before the session is closed by the get_db dependency.
The dummy hash used for missing users encodes Argon2id parameters m=65536 (KiB), t=3, p=4, so unknown-user logins also pay a full-cost hash; the login endpoint is unauthenticated.

recover_password does get_user_by_email (transaction open) and then a blocking send_email (via the emails library) before returning; the endpoint is unauthenticated. send_email sets no timeout option.
update_password_me verifies and re-hashes a password (two Argon2 operations) while holding the session.
get_db yields one Session per request; create_engine(url) sets no pool_size/max_overflow/pool_timeout, and the container runs 4 workers (CMD fastapi run --workers 4), so each worker has its own pool.
Derived: per-hash memory = 65536 KiB = 64 MiB (from the dummy-hash m parameter); N concurrent logins per worker => about N x 64 MiB transient memory. No container memory limit appears in compose.yml.
No runtime evidence (load test, profile, pool metrics) exists in the repository.

findings.conditions: Matters when concurrent login/password/recovery requests approach the sync thread pool or the SQLAlchemy pool limit of a worker (library defaults, not set in the repo), e.g. credential-stuffing, login bursts, or a slow SMTP relay. Concurrency level and SMTP latency are unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Handlers are plain def so they run in a threadpool, not on the event loop; the loop is not blocked. Argon2 libraries typically release the GIL, so hashing parallelises across threads.
Searched for pool configuration, rate limiting and background-task use for email: none found.
Hashing cost is a deliberate security choice; the fix is not to weaken it.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Argon2 cost is intentional and logins are usually a small share of traffic; if SMTP is fast and load is modest, thread and pool limits are never reached.
findings.recommendation: Release the DB connection before slow non-DB work: in authenticate, read the user then end the transaction (commit/close, or copy needed fields) before hashing; in recover_password, finish the lookup then send the email via BackgroundTasks or a queue with an explicit SMTP timeout. Set pool_size/max_overflow/pool_timeout explicitly and add rate limiting on login and recovery.

alternatives.option: Release connection before hashing/sending; send mail in a background task
alternatives.why: Removes the held resource without changing hash strength.
Raises the ceiling but multiplies by 4 workers against Postgres max_connections and does not shorten hold time.

findings.trade_offs: Background email loses synchronous error reporting; ending the transaction early needs care with ORM object expiry. Rate limiting needs shared state across 4 workers.

validation.metric: Pool checked-out count and wait time, thread-pool queue depth, and p95 latency of POST /login/access-token and /password-recovery under concurrent load
validation.expectation: Connection hold time per login drops to query time; pool wait no longer scales with hash duration.
validation.falsifier: Under a load test at expected concurrency, pool checkout wait and threadpool queueing stay near zero before the change.
validation.guard: Pool-exhaustion alert (checkout timeouts) and a staging load test.

commands.command: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname='app' GROUP BY state;
commands.purpose: Observe 'idle in transaction' connections while login load runs

findings.problem: List endpoints accept caller-supplied skip and limit with no upper bound, use OFFSET pagination, and run a separate count(*) on every page.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request work and response size should be bounded by the server, not by the caller.

evidence.statement: limit: int = 100 and skip: int = 0 are plain ints with no ge/le constraint in read_items; the page is materialised with .all() then validated item by item.

findings.conditions: Matters if a client (or abuser) requests a very large limit against a large result set; superusers see all rows. Normal frontend use is capped at 100.

counter_evidence.statement: Authenticated access only; non-superusers are limited to their own rows; the frontend uses 100.

findings.recommendation: Constrain limit with Query(ge=1, le=<max>) and consider keyset pagination if deep offsets matter.
findings.trade_offs: A maximum is a small API contract change for clients relying on larger pages.

validation.metric: Response time and size for a very large limit on a large table
validation.expectation: Request rejected or capped at the maximum.
validation.falsifier: The request already returns a validation error.
